issues.legal_issue: The benefit of doubt is available only when consideration of the entire evidence leaves a conscientious and reasonable doubt about guilt, and not merely as a matter of abundant caution or at isolated stages of the evidence.
material_facts: The appellate court found the eyewitnesses reliable but acquitted one accused as a matter of abundant caution without identifying a reasonable doubt in their evidence or in the case as a whole.
The prosecution evidence, considered as a whole, established that the accused restrained the victim while the other assailants attacked him.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court gave the benefit of doubt on a misplaced basis; the evidence did not leave a reasonable doubt, so the acquittal was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Proof beyond reasonable doubt requires a conscientious assessment of the entire evidence; a merely possible or fanciful doubt is insufficient, and the benefit-of-doubt principle should not be stretched to embrace every hesitation. The Court relied on Shivaji Sahebrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra and Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ram Kishan Rohatgi.

predicates.state_appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed against an acquittal.
predicates.reliable_eyewitness_evidence: Witnesses who observed the offence gave evidence that the court found reliable.
predicates.acquittal_based_only_on_caution_without_: The acquittal rested on caution, but the court giving it identified no reasonable doubt in the evidence or the case as a whole.
predicates.whole_record_supports_guilt_beyond_reaso: Consideration of the whole record supported guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal, reliable eyewitness evidence and a whole record supporting guilt beyond reasonable doubt make a benefit of doubt based only on caution without an identified reasonable doubt unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: A court must assess medical expert opinion for logic and probability and is not bound to accept an unsupported opinion that conflicts with reliable eyewitness evidence.
material_facts: The medical witness described a wide and long incised wound to the victim’s neck and said it was possibly caused by one blow, not two.
The eyewitnesses described the assailants striking the victim’s neck, but the medical witness gave no cogent reason for rejecting the possibility that successive strikes caused the wound.
The Court considered that successive strikes at the same location could have caused the wound and was not persuaded that the medical evidence created a reasonable doubt.
issues.conclusion: The medical witness’s unsupported opinion did not create a reasonable doubt about the prosecution’s account.
issues.legal_principle: Expert opinion is entitled to due weight but is not the last word; the court must test it for logic, objectivity and probability and may prefer a more probable view when an opinion lacks cogent support.

rule.if: criminal_homicide_case and reliable_eyewitness_account and medical_opinion_conflicts_with_that_account and medical_opinion_lacks_cogent_support and eyewitness_account_is_medically_plausible

predicates.criminal_homicide_case: The proceeding concerned a prosecution for a killing.
predicates.reliable_eyewitness_account: Witnesses who observed the killing gave an account that the court found reliable.
predicates.medical_opinion_conflicts_with_that_acco: A medical witness gave an opinion that conflicted with the eyewitness account.
predicates.medical_opinion_lacks_cogent_support: The medical witness gave no cogent reason for the conflicting opinion.
predicates.eyewitness_account_is_medically_plausibl: The eyewitness account remained a plausible explanation of the injuries.

issues.definition: In a killing prosecution, a conflicting medical opinion that lacks cogent support does not create reasonable doubt when reliable eyewitness evidence gives a medically plausible account.

issues.legal_issue: A participant who restrains a victim while others inflict a fatal attack may share their common intention and be liable for the killing with them.
material_facts: Reliable eyewitnesses saw the accused hold the victim’s legs while two others struck the victim’s neck with a sharp weapon.
The three assailants left together after the attack.
The Court found no reasonable doubt that the accused shared the other assailants’ common intention.
issues.conclusion: The accused shared the common intention to commit the killing and his conviction for murder with the other assailants was restored under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, participation in an offence in furtherance of a shared common intention supports joint liability; the Court assessed the accused’s active assistance as part of the occurrence as a whole. The conviction was under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

rule.if: group_homicide_prosecution and reliable_evidence_of_restraint_during_fatal_attack and associates_inflicted_fatal_injuries and participants_left_together

predicates.group_homicide_prosecution: The proceeding concerned a killing allegedly committed by multiple participants.
predicates.reliable_evidence_of_restraint_during_fa: Reliable evidence showed that one participant restrained the victim while the attack occurred.
predicates.associates_inflicted_fatal_injuries: Other participants inflicted the injuries that killed the victim.
predicates.participants_left_together: The participants left together after the attack.

issues.definition: In a group homicide prosecution, reliable evidence that one participant restrained the victim during a fatal attack by associates, followed by the participants leaving together, establishes common intention.
